Acannability’s Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™ (“The Table”)

Understand cannabis by its molecules —
not its strain names.

An educational resource from Acannability covering 64 cannabis plant molecules — cannabinoids, terpenes, and flavonoids selected from the hundreds of compounds identified in the cannabis plant — and what published research reports about each, across 65 health topics.

Strain names are inconsistent from grower to grower. Molecules aren’t. The Table organizes the published science around the molecules themselves, so you can see what researchers have actually studied — and how strong that evidence is.

Full Disclaimer & Terms of Use
Acannability’s Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™
Please read this before you continue

Acannability’s Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™ — “The Table” — is an educational resource from Acannability. It organizes and summarizes published scientific research on cannabis-derived molecules — cannabinoids, terpenes, and flavonoids — so you can explore what the literature reports.

It presents research findings and scientific evidence — not treatment recommendations. The Table does not provide medical advice, a diagnosis, or a prescription, and it is not a substitute for professional care. Please consult a qualified healthcare professional — a physician, pharmacist, or other licensed provider — about any medical decision.

Please review the information below, then confirm to enter.

⚠
This platform is for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice, a diagnosis, or a treatment recommendation. Always consult a licensed healthcare professional before making any health-related decision.
🔞 Age Requirement
You must be 21 years of age or older to access this platform. In jurisdictions where medical cannabis is permitted, you must be 18 or older with a valid medical recommendation. By entering, you confirm you meet the applicable age requirement for your location.
📚 Educational Purpose Only
All content on this platform is strictly for educational and informational purposes. Evidence ratings reflect the quality of published research — not clinical approval, proven efficacy, or safety for any individual. The absence of adverse findings does not imply that a molecule is safe. Most cannabis molecules remain insufficiently studied.
⚖️ Legal Compliance
Cannabis and cannabis-derived products are subject to varying federal, state, and local laws. It is your sole responsibility to understand and comply with all applicable laws in your jurisdiction before using, purchasing, or recommending any cannabis product. Nothing on this platform constitutes legal advice.
🩺 Not a Substitute for Professional Care
This platform must never replace consultation with a licensed physician, pharmacist, or other qualified healthcare provider. Cannabis compounds may interact with medications and affect individuals differently based on age, sex, genetics, and health status. Individual responses vary significantly.
🔒 Privacy, Data Handling & HIPAA
This platform runs entirely in your browser and has no backend server or database — it does not collect, store, or transmit Protected Health Information (PHI) as defined under HIPAA. Any medication list you enter in the Drug Interaction Checker exists only in your browser's temporary memory for the current session; it is never saved to a server, never transmitted over the internet, and is cleared when you end your session, close the tab, or refresh the page. If this platform is used on a shared or public device (for example, a dispensary kiosk), select End Session (shown as I'm Done — End My Session on larger screens) when finished so no information you entered remains visible to the next person. This platform is not itself a HIPAA-covered entity's medical record or communication system; organizations that are HIPAA-covered entities or business associates remain independently responsible for their own compliance obligations when using this tool in a patient-facing setting, and should consult their own legal or compliance counsel. One limited exception: the optional "Suggest an addition" feedback form. If you voluntarily choose to submit a suggestion, only the item you type (for example, the name of a medication or condition you feel is missing) is saved anonymously in this browser so our staff can review it and improve this educational resource. It is never linked to your identity — please do not enter your name or any personal health information in it. Optional research contribution: if you opt in at the end of a Guided Match, the anonymous, non-identifying details you provide (age group, sex, and city/state) are saved on this device and, where that feature is enabled, shared with Acannability’s research database to help improve this platform — never linked to your identity and never including personal or health information. What does The Table include?+

The Table includes the following features, interactive tools, and safety enhancements:

Associated Molecules Panel — When a health condition is selected, a panel appears showing which molecules are associated, organized by category (phytocannabinoids, terpenes, flavonoids). The panel always mirrors the highlighted tiles on the grid exactly.

Receptor System + Health Condition Combined Filtering — Select a receptor system (CB1, CB2, TRP, etc.) and a health condition together. Only molecules that match both filters are highlighted. Switching between receptor systems or conditions performs a complete automatic reset — no manual clearing required.

Refine Inventory Match — Available in both Health Conditions and Entourage Effect panels. Exclude specific molecule classes or individual molecules your dispensary doesn't carry so recommendations reflect only your actual inventory.

Adverse Findings Category — A new top-level sidebar category surfaces molecules with documented safety or efficacy findings from peer-reviewed literature. Each flagged molecule displays a ⚠ tile badge and a full Adverse Findings accordion in its detail panel with evidence-graded citations and PubMed links.

Prominent Disclaimer System — A bold "Not Medical Advice" ribbon is permanently visible above the grid. A full 7-section disclaimer modal (accessible from any panel) covers educational purpose, evidence grade limitations, adverse findings gaps, and professional consultation requirements. The Welcome screen now requires an informed-consent checkbox before entry.

Molecule Category Search Reset — The molecule category search dropdown now includes a one-click reset option at the top of the list.

Women's Health Conditions — New conditions added: Endometriosis, Uterine Fibroids, Dysmenorrhea, and Menopause/Perimenopause Symptoms.

New Citations — Sex-differentiated pharmacokinetics data (Moazen-Zadeh 2024 meta-regression for CBD; Piotrowska 2018 CB2 cardiac sex/age distribution for CBD and CBG) added to relevant molecule panels. CBG now maps to the Cardiovascular Health condition based on this literature.

Official Acannability™ Logo — Replaced the placeholder icon in the header, Welcome screen, and grid hero panel with the official Acannability™ wordmark.

Guided Match — A step-by-step "Why are you here today?" finder that maps your goal to the molecules research links to it, then hands you into the Periodic Table.

Quick Safety Check — An educational, private checkpoint in the Guided Match that flags situations where cannabis deserves extra caution (pregnancy, respiratory, cardiovascular, serious mental-health history, prescription medications).

Print / Save as PDF — Print or save a clean summary of your Guided Match recommendation or your Drug Interaction report.

Optional Anonymous Research Contribution — Opt in (off by default) to share a few non-identifying details (age group, sex, city/state) to support cannabis research. No personal or health information is ever collected.

What is the Guided Match, and how does "Why are you here today?" work?+

The Guided Match is a step-by-step, plain-language guide that helps you find the cannabis molecules research links to your goal — no prior knowledge needed. Open it with the 🧭 Guided Match button in the header (or the Guided tab on mobile); it also appears automatically the first time you enter.

It begins by asking who's using the table (Consumer · "I work here" for dispensary staff · Researcher, which goes straight to the full table). Consumers are then asked "Why are you here today?" with everyday options: Sleep, Pain Relief, Anxiety & Stress, Appetite & Nausea, Cancer Symptom Support, Seizures/Epilepsy, Eye Pressure/Glaucoma, Women's Health, Men's Health, Relaxation, Explore the Research, or Something Else.

From there it asks a few short, optional questions to tailor results — the kind of relief you want, your experience level, how you feel about feeling "high" (THC comfort), time of day, how fast or long you want effects, preferred format, other concerns, a quick safety check, and any medications. It ends on "Research-Linked Molecules for Your Health Topic" — the same molecules the Periodic Table highlights for your topic, tiered into Primary and Supporting by strength of evidence — then hands you into the table to explore. Leave anytime via Full table ✕ or Skip to full table.

The Guided Match is educational: it shows research-supported molecules, not products or medical advice.

What is the "quick safety check," and when might cannabis not be appropriate?+

Near the end of the Guided Match, The Table shows "A quick safety check." It is educational, stays private on your device, and never blocks you — if anything applies, it simply adds a note to review with a healthcare professional. Tap any that apply, or skip.

The situations it asks about, because published research advises extra caution:

Pregnancy, breastfeeding, or trying to conceive — current medical guidance advises avoiding cannabis; talk with your obstetric provider.

Respiratory conditions (asthma, COPD) — smoking or vaping can irritate the airways; research generally favors non-inhaled routes.

Heart or cardiovascular conditions — THC can raise heart rate and change blood pressure.

History of psychosis or a serious mental-health condition — THC has been associated with anxiety and, in some people, with triggering or worsening psychosis.

Prescription medications — cannabis can interact with some drugs; use the medication step and the Drug Interaction Checker to screen.

Age is confirmed at the entry gate (21+, or 18+ with a valid medical recommendation where permitted). These checks reflect research-based caution, not a diagnosis — always consult a licensed professional.

Can I print or save my results as a PDF?+

Yes. Four places have a print button: the Guided Match recommendation (🖨 Print / Save as PDF), the Drug Interaction Checker results (🖨 Print), any molecule tile you open (🖨 Print this molecule profile), and the Associated Molecules panel (🖨 Print this match). Each opens your device's print dialog, where you can send it to a printer or choose Save as PDF as the destination. Every printout carries the same educational-use footer and the note that individual responses vary.

The printout is a clean, ink-friendly summary carrying The Table’s letterhead, the date, and the full educational disclaimer — the rest of the interface is hidden. If it includes medications you entered, it notes that it may contain personal information, so handle it privately. Nothing is uploaded — the summary is generated on your device.

What is Demo Mode?+

Demo Mode is a staff-only presentation mode for trade-show booths, dispensary demos, and training — not part of the everyday consumer experience. It runs on a clearly labeled fictional dispensary ("Acannability Cannabis Dispensary Demo — not a licensed store") with sample inventory, so presenters can show the full platform end-to-end without touching any real store data.

It walks through a simulated journey — condition → molecules → medication check → inventory refine → a simulated point-of-sale "in-stock" product match → a sample Certificate of Analysis (COA) — plus booth dashboards showing the business case and simulated anonymous research demographics. A banner is always visible so no one mistakes it for a live store.

Demo Mode is turned off in licensed dispensary builds, and the products shown inside it are simulated sample data, not a real menu. Today the standard experience ends at the research-based molecule recommendation and the Periodic Table. As The Table is integrated with participating dispensaries, that experience is intended to continue into real inventory matching — showing which products actually on the shelf carry the molecules research links to your selected health topic.

What is the optional anonymous research contribution, and how is my privacy protected?+

You can optionally share a few anonymous, non-identifying details — age group, sex, and city/state — to help Acannability understand how people explore cannabis research and improve this educational resource. It is strictly opt-in: opting out is the default.

You share only if you choose “Share anonymously” at the end of a Guided Match — after you have seen what The Table does, not before you get in. Decline and nothing is collected. No personal or health information is ever collected, and responses are never linked to your identity. You can withdraw everything from your device anytime via Research data & privacy in the footer.

This supports future cannabis research using aggregate demographics only, while keeping you anonymous.

Is The Table medical advice? What is it for?+

No. The Table is an educational and cannabis-research reference, not medical advice. It organizes what peer-reviewed science says about cannabis molecules, receptors, conditions, and interactions — with direct links to PubMed — the U.S. National Library of Medicine’s free public research database, explained in the next question below — so consumers, caregivers, dispensary staff, healthcare professionals, and researchers can have better-informed, science-based conversations.

It does not diagnose, treat, or recommend a product or dose. Evidence grades reflect research quality, not clinical approval or proven safety, and the absence of a safety flag does not mean a molecule is safe. Always consult a licensed healthcare professional before making any health decision.

What is PubMed, and why does The Table link to it?+

PubMed is the U.S. National Library of Medicine’s free public database of over 36 million biomedical research articles — the global reference point for peer-reviewed scientific literature. It is run by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), not by Acannability, and it is free for anyone to search.

The Table links to it so you never have to take our word for anything. Every citation carries a PMID — PubMed’s permanent ID number for a study — and clicking it opens that study on PubMed so you can read the original research yourself, or bring it to a pharmacist or physician. That is the difference between a claim and a citation.

A note on what you will find there: PubMed always shows the abstract (the researchers’ own summary) for free. Some articles also offer the complete text free through PubMed Central, which The Table links to when it is available; others sit behind a publisher paywall.

How to tell what The Table has, before you click. On a molecule tile, each research area is tagged, and each tag carries a small mark: a solid dot (●) means The Table holds one or more indexed studies for that exact molecule-and-topic pairing, and a hollow dot (○) on a greyed, dashed tag means none has been indexed yet. Clicking either one opens The Table’s own notes for that pairing rather than a search engine, so a click never lands on an empty results page.

A greyed tag does not mean the molecule was a mistake. The Table decides which molecules belong to a health topic from its evidence engine, which is entirely separate from the citation database — so a molecule is never dropped from a recommendation just because a specific study has not been indexed for it. Δ9-THC and CBD remain part of the Uterine Fibroids match, for example, even where a direct study for that pairing is not yet on file. In those cases The Table says so plainly, explains that the research may still exist, and gives you PubMed search links for both the pairing and the molecule’s wider literature — rather than inventing a citation to fill the gap.

How do I use the search bars?+

Molecule Search (left): Type a molecule's symbol or name to instantly filter the grid. Examples: "CBD", "THC", "limonene", "cannabidiol". Results update in real-time as you type. Use the ↻ reset option at the top of the dropdown to clear the filter.

Condition Search (right): Select a health condition to find all molecules with evidence for that condition. The grid highlights molecules by evidence strength (strong, moderate, or emerging), and the Associated Molecules panel appears showing matched molecules by category.

Both search boxes work independently and can be combined with receptor system and evidence grade filters for precise results.

What do the boxes shown represent?+

Each of the 64 boxes represents either a molecule of the cannabis plant or a precursor acid. There are 55 molecules (cannabinoids, terpenes, flavonoids, and rare & novel cannabinoids) and 9 precursor acids shown.

A molecule is a group of atoms bonded together—the smallest unit of a chemical compound that retains its chemical properties. A precursor acid is a compound that converts into its active non-acidic form under certain conditions (e.g., THCA becomes THC when heated).

How were the boxes selected?+

Boxes were selected as molecules having known or suspected medicinal value based on Acannability’s review of published research. The selection process was led by Acannability Advisor Mr. Joseph Friedman, RPh, MBA, a Medical Cannabis Pharmacist and Pharmacology Expert. The Table has grown from 51 to 64 entries as scientific literature has matured to support additional compounds.

How were the symbols determined?+

Symbols are two-to-five letter shorthand notations based on English names, Latin names, or discoverer names. They are publicly used in the scientific literature and help scientists communicate efficiently about each molecule.

Why is the chart organized into five sections?+

The five sections reflect the common scientific categories of cannabis plant molecules: Phytocannabinoids, Terpenes, Flavonoids, Precursor Acids, and Rare / Emerging Cannabinoids. Molecules with increasing molecular weight are ordered left to right in rows (periods), similar to the traditional periodic table of elements.

What does each section represent?+

Cannabinoids interact with the body’s endocannabinoid system to regulate pain, mood, appetite, and immune function. Over 100 have been identified in cannabis.

Terpenes are aromatic organic compounds produced in cannabis trichomes alongside cannabinoids. Common examples include myrcene, limonene, and caryophyllene, and they are believed to offer therapeutic benefits.

Flavonoids are polyphenol plant compounds that some researchers propose may work together with cannabinoids and terpenes (the “Entourage Effect”); this has not been established in human studies.

Precursor Acids are biosynthetic forms of cannabinoids that convert to their active counterparts upon decarboxylation (heat exposure).

Rare / Emerging Cannabinoids are low-abundance but pharmacologically significant compounds such as THCP, CBDP, and CBND.

How were the atomic masses calculated?+

Atomic masses were determined from public references or by summing each element’s molecular mass from the chemical formula. The table is then arranged so that molecules with increasing mass are ordered from left to right in each row.

What does the evidence rating (A–D) mean?+

Grade A — Strong, replicated human clinical evidence.

Grade B — Promising human evidence, limited in scale; positive preclinical data.

Grade C — Primarily preclinical (animal or in vitro) evidence.

Grade D — Early-stage or theoretical evidence only.

What receptor systems are shown on each molecule tile?+

CB1 — Central nervous system receptor; governs psychoactivity, analgesia, antiemetic effects. (17 molecules)

CB2 — Immune/peripheral receptor; anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, neuroprotective. (22 molecules)

TRP — Pain/temperature ion channels (TRPV1, TRPA1); analgesic and anti-inflammatory. (19 molecules)

PPAR — Nuclear receptors governing metabolism and inflammation; associated with anti-tumor and metabolic effects. (19 molecules)

5HT — Serotonin receptors; anxiolytic, antidepressant, antipsychotic effects. (13 molecules)

What health conditions does The Table cover?+

The Table covers 65 health conditions across ten clinical groups (three conditions are cross-listed: Prostate Cancer under Cancer Sub-types and Men's Health; PCOS / Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome under Women's Health and Metabolic & Cardiovascular; and Testicular Cancer under Cancer Sub-types and Men's Health):

Pain & Inflammation (8): Analgesic / Pain, Neuropathic Pain, Fibromyalgia, Sickle Cell Disease, Arthritis / Joint Pain, Muscle Spasm / Spasticity, Anti-Inflammatory, Skin Health / Acne.

Neurological (14): Epilepsy / Seizures, Sleep & Insomnia, Migraine / Headache, Tourette Syndrome, Multiple Sclerosis, Neuroprotection, Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, Neurodegenerative, Autism Spectrum (ASD), Glaucoma / Ocular Pressure, Essential Tremor, Spinal Cord Injury, Traumatic Brain Injury / Post-Concussion.

Mental Health (6): Anxiety, Depression (Major Depressive Disorder), PTSD / Trauma, Stress / Cortisol, Psychosis / Schizophrenia, Bipolar Disorder.

Substance Use Disorders (2): Opioid Use Disorder, Cannabis Use Disorder.

Cancer & Immune (6): Cancer / Anti-Tumor, Antiviral / Immune, HIV/AIDS, Antibacterial, Antifungal, Antioxidant.

Gastrointestinal (4): Antiemetic / Nausea, IBD / Crohn's / Colitis, Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), Chronic Liver Disease / Cirrhosis.

Metabolic & Cardiovascular (6): Appetite Regulation, Diabetes / Blood Sugar, Cardiovascular Health, Hyperlipidemia, Bone Health / Osteoporosis, PCOS / Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome.

Women's Health (5): Endometriosis / Pelvic Pain, Uterine Fibroids, Dysmenorrhea / Menstrual Pain, Menopause / Perimenopause Symptoms, PCOS / Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome.

Men's Health (5): Prostate Cancer, Chronic Prostatitis / Pelvic Pain, Erectile Dysfunction, Male Fertility, Testicular Cancer.

Cancer Sub-types (12): Glioblastoma, Breast Cancer, Lung Cancer, Colorectal Cancer, Leukemia, Prostate Cancer, Melanoma, Pancreatic Cancer, Liver Cancer (HCC), Ovarian Cancer, Cervical Cancer, Testicular Cancer.

How is cancer sub-type research organized?+

The Table carries molecule-level citations for 11 specific cancer subtypes. Selecting any cancer sub-type from the conditions filter bar highlights all molecules with relevant published evidence. The References tab in each molecule tile provides specific citations; the Article PDF button gives direct access to primary research.

The Adverse Findings filter also surfaces known safety or efficacy findings, ensuring balanced presentation. All citations are from peer-reviewed literature and are strictly educational — not treatment recommendations.

What is the ‘Rare / Emerging’ category?+

This category recognizes low-abundance cannabis cannabinoids with unique pharmacological properties—compounds present in trace amounts but with significant receptor activity. Examples: THCP (exceptionally high CB1 affinity), CBDP, CBND, CBL, CBE, and CBLA. This category is expected to grow as cannabis science matures.

How do I use the interactive features?+

Click any molecule tile to open the full molecular profile with evidence tabs, citations, and adverse findings if applicable.

Category filter (right panel) narrows the table to one molecular group. The ⚠ Adverse Findings category shows only molecules with documented safety or efficacy findings.

Health Conditions (top button) opens the condition selector. Selecting a condition highlights tiles by evidence strength and displays the Associated Molecules panel above the grid.

Receptor System filter (bar below Health Conditions) can be combined with a health condition — only molecules matching both will be highlighted.

Entourage Effect (top button) explores potential molecular interactions for a selected condition — how molecules may work together. Most proposed combinations are supported by preclinical or limited human research.

Evidence filter (bar below Health Conditions) narrows highlights by A/B/C/D grade.

Reset button (end of Evidence bar) clears all active filters at once.

Getting around. The desktop header holds two search bars plus 🧭 Guided Match, Show Health Conditions, ⬢ Entourage Effect, 💊 Drug Interactions, and ↩ New Session. On phones, a bottom tab bar gives Guided · Molecules · Conditions · Interactions · Entourage · Info. Move into the Guided Match anytime with the 🧭 button or Guided tab, and return with Full table ✕.

Shared or kiosk device. Use ↩ New Session (or "I'm Done") to reset to the disclaimer for the next visitor; an inactivity timer also resets the session automatically after a short idle period. On phones, swipe down to dismiss a molecule sheet and swipe left/right to move between molecules.

What does the Drug Interaction Checker do?+

Click 💊 Drug Interactions in the header to open the checker. It has two modes: Single Medication, for looking up one drug at a time, and My Medication List, which lets you build a list of several medications and check them together.

Drug-Cannabis interactions show how a searched medication interacts with specific cannabis molecules — severity (major/moderate/minor), evidence grade (A–D), mechanism, expected effect, and monitoring guidance, with PubMed citations where available.

Drug-Drug interactions appear automatically once your medication list has two or more drugs that interact directly with each other, independent of cannabis.

A molecule's detail panel also has its own 💊 Drug Interactions tab, listing every medication known to interact with that specific molecule.

You can 🖨 Print the results (or save them as a PDF) for your pharmacist or physician. This tool is an educational reference only and does not replace advice from a licensed professional.

What is the Associated Molecules panel?+

When you pick a health condition, The Table highlights every molecule that published research links to it. The Associated Molecules panel is simply a plain-language list of those highlighted molecules, gathered in one place — so you don’t have to hunt for them across the table. It appears just below the Health Conditions section.

How to read it: the molecules are grouped by type — cannabinoids, terpenes, and flavonoids — and ordered so the best-supported ones stand out. Think of it as your shortlist for that condition: the molecules to look for on product labels and to talk through with a pharmacist or provider. Click any molecule to see its full profile, evidence grade, and research citations.

The list always matches the tiles glowing on the table. If you also choose a receptor system (such as CB1 or CB2), it narrows to the molecules that fit both your condition and that receptor, and it refreshes automatically whenever you change a selection — so what you see is always up to date.

Use the ⚙ Refine Inventory Match button at the top of the panel to hide molecules a dispensary doesn’t carry, so your shortlist reflects only what’s actually available to buy.

How do Receptor System filters work with Health Conditions?+

Receptor System filters (CB1, CB2, TRP, 5-HT, PPAR) and Health Condition filters work independently but can be combined. When both are active, only molecules that match the selected condition and interact with the selected receptor system are highlighted on the grid.

Switching from one receptor to another automatically performs a complete reset — no stale highlights carry over. The Associated Molecules panel updates instantly to reflect the new combined selection. Use the × Reset button to clear all filters at once and return to the default view.

A receptor filter narrows the table — it does not define relevance. The five systems shown are the best-characterised targets for these molecules, but they are not the only ones those molecules act through. Some well-documented effects run through other pathways entirely, or through mechanisms not yet identified. A published example sits in this build: in the prostate cancer research cited for CBD, the effect was not blocked by CB1 or CB2 antagonists, a TRPV1 blocker or a GPR55 agonist — CBD was acting through none of the systems in this bar. So filtering by receptor first can hide molecules whose evidence for your condition is real but runs by another route. When you are exploring a health condition, start with the condition and treat receptor as a secondary lens.

What is Refine Inventory Match?+

Refine Inventory Match is a tool for dispensary professionals and pharmacists. It lets you exclude specific molecule classes (e.g., all flavonoids) or individual molecules (e.g., THCV) from the recommendation if your dispensary doesn't carry products containing them.

Once exclusions are set, the Associated Molecules panel and Entourage Effect analysis both recalculate instantly to draw recommendations only from molecules your inventory can actually fulfill. Exclusions are shared across both Health Conditions and Entourage Effect panels.

Today this is a manual refinement — staff uncheck what the store doesn't carry (or load the store's catalogue by CSV). Live, real-time integration — where The Table would connect directly to a dispensary's point-of-sale (POS) / seed-to-sale system to rank in-stock products automatically and show each product's actual lab report (COA) — is in development, and is previewed today only as a simulation in Demo Mode.

What are Adverse Findings, and how are they different from therapeutic findings?+

Adverse Findings are documented safety signals, risk associations, known side effects, or trials that found no benefit, from peer-reviewed scientific literature. They are graded on the same A–D evidence scale used for therapeutic findings, so users can assess their strength. Every health topic presents them the same way — one evidence-graded, cited format across the whole resource, so no condition looks more or less serious than the evidence warrants. Any molecule with a documented finding for the topic you selected is also highlighted in red on the grid.

Molecules with documented adverse findings display a red ⚠ badge on their tile. Clicking the tile shows an Adverse Findings section in the detail panel with a plain-language summary and direct PubMed citation links.

Important: The absence of a ⚠ badge does not mean a molecule is safe — most cannabis molecules have not yet been sufficiently studied for adverse effects. As new research emerges, additional molecules will be flagged. This platform is for educational use only; always consult a licensed healthcare professional.

Some citations with weak study designs (e.g., ecological studies) appear as footnotes rather than full adverse entries, per Acannability editorial policy.

Why can the same product affect two people differently?+

Because people are not interchangeable. How much of a cannabis molecule reaches your bloodstream — and how long it stays there — varies from person to person, so the same product at the same dose can affect two people differently. Factors include genetics (inherited differences in the liver enzymes that process cannabinoids), metabolism, prior cannabis exposure (regular use can change sensitivity over time), route of administration (inhaled, oral, sublingual, topical and transdermal forms differ substantially in how much reaches the bloodstream and how fast), concurrent medications, and individual bioavailability.

You will find this stated in three places: on any molecule tile you open, on the Guided Match recommendation, and on every printout. Published findings describe what researchers observed in study populations and should not be interpreted as predicting how any individual will respond. This is educational information, not dosing guidance.

How does inventory matching work, and what is coming next?+

Today, matching is manual and honest about it: pick a health topic, and the Associated Molecules panel lists every molecule published research links to it. Use ⚙ Refine Inventory Match to remove molecules or whole categories your dispensary does not carry, and the match updates instantly. Dispensary staff can also import a stock list as a CSV.

What is coming is automation. With a point-of-sale connection, in-stock ranking becomes live instead of manual. With certificate-of-analysis (COA) data, matching reaches past cannabinoids into the terpene profile, which is where most of the differentiation actually sits. Both are previewed in Demo Mode today.

One honest limit worth knowing: dispensary menus publish cannabinoid content for every product, terpene content for some, and flavonoid content for none. Where a product publishes no lab data for a molecule, The Table reports that it cannot verify a match rather than guessing.

What happens before I get to the table?+

Two short screens. First a welcome page introducing what this educational resource is, with four plain-language acknowledgements to confirm. Second the full disclaimer, with all six acknowledgements and the same “I Agree & Enter” confirmation as before. Nothing was removed from the disclaimer — the welcome screen adds a friendlier front door in front of it. The point of the checkpoint is unchanged: every visitor actively acknowledges that this is an educational resource, not medical advice. The optional anonymous research contribution is not part of getting in; The Table offers it at the end of a Guided Match instead.

Key limitations users confirm before entering:

Evidence grades ≠ clinical approval — An "A" grade means human trial data exists, not that the treatment is FDA-approved or right for you.

Most molecules are understudied — Especially for adverse effects. Absence of a safety flag ≠ proven safe.

Consult a professional — Individual responses vary. A pharmacist, physician, or specialist should guide any health decision.

The Full Disclaimer (accessible via the red ribbon or any molecule panel) covers all seven limitation categories in detail.

What is the Entourage Effect?+

A concept in cannabis pharmacology describing how the plant’s many molecules—cannabinoids, terpenes, and flavonoids—may work synergistically, producing effects greater than any isolated compound alone. Popularized by Dr. Raphael Mechoulam, it influences how clinicians and product developers think about whole-plant versus isolate therapies. It remains a hypothesis: most of the research is preclinical, and a combined clinical benefit has not been established. The Table’s Entourage Effect explorer, Potential Molecular Interactions, shows proposed combinations for a health topic and how strong the underlying evidence is.

How should this chart be used by consumers?+

The chart serves as a common scientific language for consumers, caregivers, and industry participants. Uses include:

Product Selection — Compare molecule claims on product labels against published evidence.

Molecule Identification — Click any molecule tile for name, mass, evidence rating, receptors, and citations.

Research — Scientists may use the table as a reference with direct links to primary literature PDFs.

Education — Introduce students and practitioners to the fundamental compounds of the cannabis plant.

Is this chart proprietary to Acannability?+

Yes. The Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™ was developed by Acannability through the work of Advisor Joseph Friedman, RPh, MBA. It is free to use by Acannability members and available to others by copyright license acknowledgement. A printable version is available at Acannability.com.

Disclaimer+

The Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™ is an educational reference tool and should never be used as a source of medical advice. Medical decisions and treatments must be based solely on the guidance of qualified healthcare professionals. Always consult a licensed medical practitioner before making any health-related decisions.

Acannability’s Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™
Is The Table medical advice? What is it for?+

No. The Table is an educational and cannabis-research reference, not medical advice. It organizes what peer-reviewed science says about cannabis molecules, receptors, conditions, and interactions — with direct links to PubMed — the U.S. National Library of Medicine’s free public research database, explained in the next question below — so consumers, caregivers, dispensary staff, healthcare professionals, and researchers can have better-informed, science-based conversations.

It does not diagnose, treat, or recommend a product or a dose. Evidence grades reflect research quality, not clinical approval or proven safety, and the absence of a safety flag does not mean a molecule is safe. Always consult a licensed healthcare professional before making any health decision.

What is PubMed, and why does The Table link to it?+

PubMed is the U.S. National Library of Medicine’s free public database of over 36 million biomedical research articles — the global reference point for peer-reviewed scientific literature. It is run by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), not by Acannability, and it is free for anyone to search.

The Table links to it so you never have to take our word for anything. Every citation carries a PMID — PubMed’s permanent ID number for a study — and clicking it opens that study on PubMed so you can read the original research yourself, or bring it to a pharmacist or physician. That is the difference between a claim and a citation.

A note on what you will find there: PubMed always shows the abstract (the researchers’ own summary) for free. Some articles also offer the complete text free through PubMed Central, which The Table links to when it is available; others sit behind a publisher paywall.

How to tell what The Table has, before you click. On a molecule tile, each research area is tagged, and each tag carries a small mark: a solid dot (●) means The Table holds one or more indexed studies for that exact molecule-and-topic pairing, and a hollow dot (○) on a greyed, dashed tag means none has been indexed yet. Clicking either one opens The Table’s own notes for that pairing rather than a search engine, so a click never lands on an empty results page.

A greyed tag does not mean the molecule was a mistake. The Table decides which molecules belong to a health topic from its evidence engine, which is entirely separate from the citation database — so a molecule is never dropped from a recommendation just because a specific study has not been indexed for it. Δ9-THC and CBD remain part of the Uterine Fibroids match, for example, even where a direct study for that pairing is not yet on file. In those cases The Table says so plainly, explains that the research may still exist, and gives you PubMed search links for both the pairing and the molecule’s wider literature — rather than inventing a citation to fill the gap.

What does The Table include?+

The Table includes the following features, interactive tools, and safety enhancements:

Associated Molecules Panel. When a health condition is selected, a panel appears between the Health Conditions section and the Receptor Systems bar, showing associated molecules organized by category (phytocannabinoids, terpenes, flavonoids, etc.). The panel always mirrors the highlighted tiles on the grid exactly, including when a Receptor System filter is also active.

Receptor System + Health Condition Combined Filtering. Select a receptor system (CB1, CB2, TRP, etc.) together with a health condition. Only molecules matching both filters are highlighted. Switching between selections performs a complete automatic reset — no manual clearing required. A × Reset button also clears all filters at once.

Refine Inventory Match. Available in both Health Conditions and Entourage Effect panels, this feature allows dispensary staff or consumers to exclude specific molecule classes or individual molecules not currently in the dispensary’s inventory. Recommendations instantly recalculate to reflect only what is available.

Adverse Findings Category. A new top-level sidebar category surfaces molecules with documented safety or efficacy findings from peer-reviewed literature. Each flagged molecule displays a ⚠ tile badge and a full Adverse Findings section in its detail panel with evidence-graded citations and direct PubMed links. The absence of a ⚠ badge does not mean a molecule is safe — it means adverse effects have not yet been sufficiently studied.

Prominent Disclaimer System. A “Not Medical Advice” ribbon is permanently visible above the grid. A full seven-section disclaimer modal covers educational purpose, evidence grade limitations, adverse findings gaps, and professional consultation requirements. The Welcome screen now requires an informed-consent checkbox before entry.

Women’s Health Conditions. Four new conditions added: Endometriosis, Uterine Fibroids, Dysmenorrhea, and Menopause/Perimenopause Symptoms.

New Citations. Sex-differentiated pharmacokinetics data added for CBD (Moazen-Zadeh 2024 meta-regression on sex-dependent absorption) and CBG (Piotrowska 2018 CB2 cardiac receptor sex/age distribution). CBG now maps to the Cardiovascular Health condition.

Official Acannability™ Logo. The official Acannability™ wordmark now appears in the header, Welcome screen, and grid hero panel.

Guided Match. A step-by-step "Why are you here today?" finder that maps your goal to the molecules research links to it, then hands you into the Periodic Table.

Quick Safety Check. An educational, private checkpoint in the Guided Match that flags situations where cannabis deserves extra caution (pregnancy, respiratory, cardiovascular, serious mental-health history, prescription medications).

Print / Save as PDF. Print or save a clean summary of your Guided Match recommendation or your Drug Interaction report.

Optional Anonymous Research Contribution. Opt in (off by default) to share a few non-identifying details (age group, sex, city/state) to support cannabis research. No personal or health information is ever collected.

What is the Guided Match, and how does "Why are you here today?" work?+

The Guided Match is a step-by-step, plain-language guide that helps you find the cannabis molecules research links to your goal — no prior knowledge needed. Open it with the 🧭 Guided Match button in the header (or the Guided tab on mobile); it also appears automatically the first time you enter.

It begins by asking who's using the table (Consumer · "I work here" for dispensary staff · Researcher, which goes straight to the full table). Consumers are then asked "Why are you here today?" with everyday options: Sleep, Pain Relief, Anxiety & Stress, Appetite & Nausea, Cancer Symptom Support, Seizures/Epilepsy, Eye Pressure/Glaucoma, Women's Health, Men's Health, Relaxation, Explore the Research, or Something Else.

From there it asks a few short, optional questions to tailor results — the kind of relief you want, your experience level, how you feel about feeling "high" (THC comfort), time of day, how fast or long you want effects, preferred format, other concerns, a quick safety check, and any medications. It ends on "Research-Linked Molecules for Your Health Topic" — the same molecules the Periodic Table highlights for your topic, tiered into Primary and Supporting by strength of evidence — then hands you into the table to explore. Leave anytime via Full table ✕ or Skip to full table.

The Guided Match is educational: it shows research-supported molecules, not products or medical advice.

What is the "quick safety check," and when might cannabis not be appropriate?+

Near the end of the Guided Match, The Table shows "A quick safety check." It is educational, stays private on your device, and never blocks you — if anything applies, it simply adds a note to review with a healthcare professional. Tap any that apply, or skip.

The situations it asks about, because published research advises extra caution:

Pregnancy, breastfeeding, or trying to conceive — current medical guidance advises avoiding cannabis; talk with your obstetric provider.

Respiratory conditions (asthma, COPD) — smoking or vaping can irritate the airways; research generally favors non-inhaled routes.

Heart or cardiovascular conditions — THC can raise heart rate and change blood pressure.

History of psychosis or a serious mental-health condition — THC has been associated with anxiety and, in some people, with triggering or worsening psychosis.

Prescription medications — cannabis can interact with some drugs; use the medication step and the Drug Interaction Checker to screen.

Age is confirmed at the entry gate (21+, or 18+ with a valid medical recommendation where permitted). These checks reflect research-based caution, not a diagnosis — always consult a licensed professional.

Can I print or save my results as a PDF?+

Yes. Four places have a print button: the Guided Match recommendation (🖨 Print / Save as PDF), the Drug Interaction Checker results (🖨 Print), any molecule tile you open (🖨 Print this molecule profile), and the Associated Molecules panel (🖨 Print this match). Each opens your device's native print dialog, where you can send it to a printer or choose Save as PDF as the destination. Every printout carries the same educational-use footer and the note that individual responses vary.

The printout is a clean, ink-friendly summary carrying The Table’s letterhead, the date, and the full educational disclaimer — the rest of the interface is hidden. If it includes medications you entered, it notes that the page may contain personal information, so please handle it privately. Nothing is uploaded — the summary is generated on your device.

What is Demo Mode?+

Demo Mode is a staff-only presentation mode for trade-show booths, dispensary demos, and training — not part of the everyday consumer experience. It runs on a clearly labeled fictional dispensary ("Acannability Cannabis Dispensary Demo — not a licensed store") with sample inventory, so presenters can show the full platform end-to-end without touching any real store data.

It walks through a simulated journey — condition → molecules → medication check → inventory refine → a simulated point-of-sale "in-stock" product match → a sample Certificate of Analysis (COA) — plus booth dashboards showing the business case and simulated anonymous research demographics. A banner is always visible so no one mistakes it for a live store, and everything is clearly marked "sample" or "simulated."

Demo Mode is turned off in licensed dispensary builds, and the products shown inside it are simulated sample data, not a real menu. Today the standard experience ends at the research-based molecule recommendation and the Periodic Table. As The Table is integrated with participating dispensaries, that experience is intended to continue into real inventory matching — showing which products actually on the shelf carry the molecules research links to your selected health topic.

What is the optional anonymous research contribution, and how is my privacy protected?+

You can optionally share a few anonymous, non-identifying details — age group, sex, and city/state — to help Acannability understand how people explore cannabis research and improve this educational resource. It is strictly opt-in: opting out is the default.

You share only if you choose “Share anonymously” at the end of a Guided Match — after you have seen what The Table does, not before you get in. Decline and nothing is collected. No personal or health information is ever collected, and responses are never linked to your identity. You can withdraw everything from your device at any time via Research data & privacy in the footer.

This supports future cannabis research using aggregate demographics only, while keeping you anonymous.

What do the boxes shown represent?+

Each of the 64 boxes on the Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™ chart represents either a molecule of the cannabis plant or a precursor acid. There are 55 molecules (cannabinoids, terpenes, flavonoids, and rare & novel cannabinoids) and 9 precursor acids shown. A molecule and a precursor acid are two different chemical entities with distinct characteristics and functions.

A molecule is a group of atoms bonded together. It is the smallest unit of a chemical compound that retains the chemical properties of that compound. Molecules can be simple, containing only a few atoms, or complex, consisting of hundreds or thousands of atoms.

A precursor acid refers to a chemical compound that participates in a chemical reaction producing other compounds. Under certain conditions it can convert the molecule into its non-acidic form. Precursor acids typically contain one or more acidic functional groups, such as a carboxyl group (–COOH).

For example, THCa is the acidic form of THC. Although THCa does have medicinal properties, it does not have psychoactive properties. The process of decarboxylation requires exposure to heat. When vaporizing or smoking, high temperatures quickly decarboxylate THCa to THC, enabling the body to absorb it through the lungs. Oxygen exposure can also contribute to the decarboxylation process.

How were the boxes selected?+

The boxes shown were selected as molecules having known or suspected medicinal value based on Acannability’s review of published research. The selection process was led by Acannability Advisor Mr. Joseph Friedman, RPh, MBA, a Medical Cannabis Pharmacist and Pharmacology Expert. Mr. Friedman was the founding member at Professional Dispensaries of Illinois Medical LLC, a medical cannabis dispensary owned and operated by pharmacists, nurses, and cannabis experts. He is an expert in the scientific, legal, social, political, and financial challenges facing U.S. entrants to the burgeoning medical cannabis industry. Mr. Friedman has contributed to several published articles in local and national publications and continually advocates for pharmacists’ involvement in the medical cannabis industry.

The Table has grown from 51 to 64 entries, adding 13 newly characterized or emerging molecules—particularly from the Rare / Emerging cannabinoid category—as scientific literature has matured to support their inclusion.

How were the symbols determined and what do they mean?+

The symbols on the Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™ chart are shorthand notations used to represent each molecule. These symbols are two to five letters, and they play a crucial role in identifying and organizing the entries in a systematic manner. The symbols are based on the English names, Latin names, or their discoverer’s names, and are publicly used in the scientific literature. They help chemists and scientists communicate efficiently and unambiguously about molecules and precursor acids.

Why is the chart organized into five sections?+

The organization of the Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™ chart was based on the common scientific assessment of the cannabis plant as a whole. Cannabinoids (phytocannabinoids and rare & novel variants), terpenes, flavonoids, and precursor acids are commonly recognized categories. The Table carries a dedicated Rare / Emerging section to reflect the growing scientific literature on less-characterized but clinically significant cannabis compounds. The periodic table’s arrangement is such that molecules with increasing molecular weight are ordered from left to right in rows (periods).

What does each section represent?+

A cannabinoid is a type of chemical compound found in the cannabis plant, as well as in some other plants and in the human body. Cannabinoids interact with the body’s endocannabinoid system, which is involved in regulating a wide range of physiological processes such as pain, mood, appetite, and immune function. There are over 100 cannabinoids identified in the cannabis plant, including THC and CBD, which are the most well-known.

Terpenes are a large and diverse class of organic compounds found in many plants, including cannabis. Produced in the same glandular trichomes as cannabinoids, they contribute to aroma and flavor and are believed to have a range of potential therapeutic benefits. Common examples include myrcene, limonene, pinene, and caryophyllene.

Flavonoids are plant compounds belonging to the larger class of polyphenols, widely distributed in fruits, vegetables, and medicinal plants including cannabis. Several flavonoids retain medicinal value that may work in concert with cannabinoids and terpenes to enhance the medical properties of the cannabis plant—commonly known as the “Entourage Effect.”

Precursor Acids are the biosynthetic forms of cannabinoids, produced by the plant before decarboxylation converts them into their active counterparts (e.g., THCA becomes THC when heated).

Rare / Emerging Cannabinoids represent a growing category of less-abundant but scientifically significant cannabis compounds such as THCP, CBDP, CBND, and others, where emerging research suggests unique pharmacological activity beyond classic cannabinoids.

How were the atomic masses calculated?+

The atomic masses shown in the Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™ chart were determined by public references or the chemical formula. In the case of the latter, each element’s molecular mass was identified and totaled. For example, for water (H2O), two hydrogen atoms with mass ≈1 each and one oxygen atom with mass ≈16 total 18 for the molecule. After identifying or calculating the atomic masses of all the molecules, the table was constructed to reflect an objective structure, similar to the traditional periodic table of elements.

What does the evidence rating shown on each molecule tile mean?+

Each molecule tile in The Table displays a letter-grade evidence rating (A, B, C, or D) in the upper-right corner, reflecting the strength of published clinical and preclinical research supporting the molecule’s therapeutic applications:

Grade A — Strong, replicated human clinical evidence with broad scientific consensus.

Grade B — Promising human evidence, though limited in scale or scope; positive preclinical data supports further investigation.

Grade C — Primarily preclinical (animal or in vitro) evidence with limited human studies to date.

Grade D — Early-stage or theoretical evidence only; molecule is of emerging scientific interest.

Evidence ratings are assigned by Acannability based on review of the published literature and are updated as new research becomes available.

What receptor systems are shown on each molecule tile?+

The Table identifies which of five major receptor systems each molecule is known to engage. These receptor interactions are central to understanding how each compound produces its physiological effects:

CB1 (Cannabinoid Receptor 1) — Present primarily in the central nervous system. CB1 activation is responsible for the psychoactive effects of THC, as well as analgesia, appetite stimulation, and antiemetic properties. 17 molecules in the table engage CB1.

CB2 (Cannabinoid Receptor 2) — Found predominantly in immune tissues and peripheral organs. CB2 activation is associated with anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and neuroprotective effects, typically without psychoactivity. 22 molecules engage CB2.

TRP (Transient Receptor Potential Channels) — Including TRPV1 and TRPA1, these ion channels are involved in pain signaling, temperature sensation, and inflammation. Several terpenes and cannabinoids modulate TRP channels to produce analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects. 19 molecules engage TRP channels.

PPAR (Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptors) — Nuclear receptors involved in metabolism, inflammation regulation, and cell growth. PPAR activation by certain cannabinoids and flavonoids has been associated with anti-tumor, anti-diabetic, and cardiovascular effects. 19 molecules engage PPAR receptors.

5HT (Serotonin Receptors) — Particularly 5HT1A, serotonin receptor modulation is associated with anxiolytic, antidepressant, and antipsychotic effects. CBD is among the most studied molecules for 5HT activity. 13 molecules engage serotonin receptors.

Receptor data is based on published pharmacological literature. A single molecule may engage multiple receptor systems simultaneously.

What health conditions does The Table cover?+

The Table covers 65 health conditions, organized across ten clinical groups — three conditions are cross-listed: Prostate Cancer under Cancer Sub-types and Men's Health; PCOS / Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome under Women's Health and Metabolic & Cardiovascular; and Testicular Cancer under Cancer Sub-types and Men's Health:

Pain & Inflammation (8 conditions): Analgesic / Pain, Neuropathic Pain, Fibromyalgia, Sickle Cell Disease, Arthritis / Joint Pain, Muscle Spasm / Spasticity, Anti-Inflammatory, Skin Health / Acne.

Neurological (14 conditions): Epilepsy / Seizures, Sleep & Insomnia, Migraine / Headache, Tourette Syndrome, Multiple Sclerosis, Neuroprotection, Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, Neurodegenerative, Autism Spectrum (ASD), Glaucoma / Ocular Pressure, Essential Tremor, Spinal Cord Injury, Traumatic Brain Injury / Post-Concussion.

Mental Health (6 conditions): Anxiety, Depression (Major Depressive Disorder), PTSD / Trauma, Stress / Cortisol, Psychosis / Schizophrenia, Bipolar Disorder.

Substance Use Disorders (2 conditions): Opioid Use Disorder, Cannabis Use Disorder.

Cancer & Immune (6 conditions): Cancer / Anti-Tumor, Antiviral / Immune, HIV/AIDS, Antibacterial, Antifungal, Antioxidant.

Gastrointestinal (4 conditions): Antiemetic / Nausea, IBD / Crohn's / Colitis, Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), Chronic Liver Disease / Cirrhosis.

Metabolic & Cardiovascular (6 conditions): Appetite Regulation, Diabetes / Blood Sugar, Cardiovascular Health, Hyperlipidemia, Bone Health / Osteoporosis, PCOS / Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome.

Women's Health (5 conditions): Endometriosis / Pelvic Pain, Uterine Fibroids, Dysmenorrhea / Menstrual Pain, Menopause / Perimenopause Symptoms, PCOS / Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome.

Men's Health (5 conditions): Prostate Cancer, Chronic Prostatitis / Pelvic Pain, Erectile Dysfunction, Male Fertility, Testicular Cancer.

Cancer Sub-types (12 specific types): Glioblastoma, Breast Cancer, Lung Cancer, Colorectal Cancer, Leukemia, Prostate Cancer, Melanoma, Pancreatic Cancer, Liver Cancer (HCC), Ovarian Cancer, Cervical Cancer, Testicular Cancer.

Selecting any condition in the filter bar highlights which molecules have published research supporting activity in that area, along with a relevance score based on the depth of the evidence.

How is cancer sub-type research organized in this table?+

The Table carries molecule-level citations for 11 specific cancer subtypes. For each cancer type, the table identifies which of the 64 molecules have published preclinical or clinical evidence of anti-tumor activity, along with a relevance score reflecting the depth and quality of that research.

The 11 cancer subtypes covered are: Glioblastoma, Breast Cancer, Lung Cancer, Colorectal Cancer, Leukemia, Prostate Cancer, Melanoma, Pancreatic Cancer, Liver Cancer (HCC), Ovarian Cancer, and Cervical Cancer.

To explore cancer-specific research, select any cancer sub-type from the conditions filter bar. The table will highlight all molecules with relevant published evidence. Clicking any highlighted molecule tile opens the full molecular profile, where the References tab provides specific citations and the linked Article PDF gives direct access to primary research.

Importantly, the Adverse Findings filter surfaces published safety or efficacy findings and known risks—ensuring that cancer-related research is presented in full clinical context, not just benefit data.

All cancer research citations in The Table are drawn from peer-reviewed scientific literature. This information is strictly educational and does not constitute medical advice or treatment recommendations.

What is the ‘Rare / Emerging’ cannabinoid category?+

The Rare / Emerging category recognizes a growing body of scientific literature on cannabis-derived cannabinoids that are present in very small concentrations in the plant but exhibit unique and potentially significant pharmacological properties.

Examples include Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabiphorol (THCP), which has demonstrated a binding affinity for CB1 receptors significantly higher than THC, and Cannabidiphorol (CBDP), the propyl-chain analog of CBD. Others include Cannabinodiol (CBND), Cannabicyclol (CBL), Cannabielsoin (CBE), and Cannabicyclolic Acid (CBLA).

As cannabis science matures, Acannability expects this category to grow as additional rare compounds are characterized and their clinical relevance is established.

How do I use the interactive features of this table?+

Click any molecule tile to open that molecule’s full detail panel. The panel displays the molecule’s symbol, full name, molecular mass, evidence rating, and receptor targets.

Detail panel tabs organize information into therapeutic findings, Adverse/Safety findings, and peer-reviewed References with direct PubMed links.

Category filter (right sidebar) narrows the table to a single molecular category. The ⚠ Adverse Findings category shows only molecules with documented safety or efficacy findings.

Health Conditions (top button) opens the condition selector. Selecting a condition highlights tiles by evidence strength and shows the Associated Molecules panel above the Receptor Systems bar.

Receptor System filter (below Health Conditions) can be combined with a condition — only molecules matching both will be highlighted. Use × Reset to clear all filters at once.

Refine Inventory Match (in the Associated Molecules panel) lets dispensaries or consumers exclude molecules not in current inventory, so recommendations reflect only what’s available.

Entourage Effect (top button) explores potential molecular interactions for a selected condition — how molecules may work together. Most proposed combinations are supported by preclinical or limited human research.

Getting around. The desktop header holds two search bars plus 🧭 Guided Match, Show Health Conditions, ⬢ Entourage Effect, 💊 Drug Interactions, and ↩ New Session. On phones, a bottom tab bar gives Guided · Molecules · Conditions · Interactions · Entourage · Info. Move into the Guided Match anytime with the 🧭 button or Guided tab, and return to the grid with Full table ✕ or Explore these in the Periodic Table →.

Shared or kiosk device. Use ↩ New Session (or "I'm Done") to reset to the disclaimer for the next visitor; an inactivity timer also resets the session automatically after a short idle period. On phones, swipe down to dismiss a molecule sheet and swipe left/right to move between molecules.

The table is optimised for desktop viewing. On smaller screens, the grid scrolls horizontally.

What does the Drug Interaction Checker do?+

Click 💊 Drug Interactions in the header to open the checker. It offers two modes: Single Medication, for looking up one drug at a time, and My Medication List, which lets you add several medications and check them together.

Drug-Cannabis interactions show how a searched medication interacts with specific cannabis molecules — severity (major/moderate/minor), evidence grade (A=Clinical, B=Observational, C=Preclinical, D=Theoretical), mechanism, expected effect, and monitoring guidance, with PubMed links where available.

Drug-Drug interactions appear automatically when your medication list contains two or more drugs that interact directly with each other, independent of any cannabis molecule.

The database covers common medication classes including antibiotics and cancer chemotherapy agents, alongside standard drug classes. A search that returns “Not found in local database” simply means that drug hasn’t been added yet — coverage is continually expanded.

Any molecule’s detail panel also includes its own 💊 Drug Interactions tab, listing every medication with a known interaction for that specific molecule.

You can 🖨 Print the interaction results — or save them as a PDF — to share with your pharmacist or physician.

This tool is for educational reference only and does not replace advice from a licensed pharmacist or physician.

What is the Associated Molecules panel?+

When you pick a health condition, The Table highlights every molecule that published research links to it. The Associated Molecules panel is simply a plain-language list of those highlighted molecules, gathered in one place — so you don’t have to hunt for them across the table. It appears just below the Health Conditions section.

How to read it: the molecules are grouped by type — cannabinoids, terpenes, and flavonoids — and ordered so the best-supported ones stand out. Think of it as your shortlist for that condition: the molecules to look for on product labels and to talk through with a pharmacist or provider. Click any molecule to see its full profile, evidence grade, and research citations.

The list always matches the tiles glowing on the table. If you also choose a receptor system (such as CB1 or CB2), it narrows to the molecules that fit both your condition and that receptor, and it refreshes automatically whenever you change a selection — so what you see is always up to date.

Use the ⚙ Refine Inventory Match button at the top of the panel to hide molecules a dispensary doesn’t carry, so your shortlist reflects only what’s actually available to buy.

How do Receptor System filters work with Health Conditions?+

Receptor System filters (CB1, CB2, TRP, 5-HT, PPAR) and Health Condition filters work independently but can be combined. When both are active, only molecules that match the selected condition and interact with the selected receptor system are highlighted on the grid.

Switching from one receptor to another automatically performs a complete reset — no stale highlights carry over from a previous selection. The Associated Molecules panel updates instantly to reflect the new combined selection. Use the × Reset button to clear all active filters at once and return the table to its default view.

A receptor filter narrows the table — it does not define relevance. The five systems shown are the best-characterised targets for these molecules, but they are not the only ones those molecules act through. Some well-documented effects run through other pathways entirely, or through mechanisms not yet identified. A published example sits in this build: in the prostate cancer research cited for CBD, the effect was not blocked by CB1 or CB2 antagonists, a TRPV1 blocker or a GPR55 agonist — CBD was acting through none of the systems in this bar. So filtering by receptor first can hide molecules whose evidence for your condition is real but runs by another route. When you are exploring a health condition, start with the condition and treat receptor as a secondary lens.

What is Refine Inventory Match?+

Refine Inventory Match is a dispensary inventory tool. It lets staff or consumers exclude specific molecule classes (e.g., all flavonoids) or individual molecules (e.g., THCV) from the recommendation when a dispensary does not carry products containing them.

Once exclusions are set, the Associated Molecules panel and Entourage Effect analysis both recalculate instantly to reflect only molecules the dispensary’s current inventory can fulfill. Exclusions apply across both the Health Conditions and Entourage Effect panels simultaneously.

Today this is a manual refinement — staff uncheck what the store doesn’t carry, or load the store’s catalogue by CSV. Live, real-time integration — where The Table would connect directly to a dispensary’s point-of-sale (POS) / seed-to-sale system to rank in-stock products automatically and show each product’s actual lab report (COA) — is in development, and is previewed today only as a simulation in Demo Mode. See the consumer-focused question below for how this helps you find the right product.

How does Refine Inventory Match help me find the right product at my dispensary?+

Refine Inventory Match lets your dispensary narrow the molecules that published research links to your selected health topic to the ones its products can actually provide. Today this is done by hand; an automatic connection to a dispensary’s point-of-sale (POS) and inventory system is in development.

Here is the challenge Refine Inventory Match solves: the science may recommend five molecules for your condition, but your dispensary may only carry products containing three of them today. Without this feature, you might leave with a product that is missing a key molecule, reducing how closely its composition matches the research-linked molecules.

How it works for you:

Step 1 — Start with the science. Select your health condition (e.g., Anxiety, Pain, Sleep). The platform highlights every molecule with published evidence for that condition and shows the Associated Molecules panel.

Step 2 — Refine to what’s in stock. Your dispensary’s staff (or you, with their guidance) clicks Refine Inventory Match and unchecks any molecule classes or specific molecules not available in today’s inventory. The recommendation instantly recalculates.

Step 3 — Get a more precise match. The updated Associated Molecules panel shows only what your dispensary can actually provide, so the products you compare are more likely to contain the research-linked molecules — even on a day when inventory is limited.

Note: Today, Refine Inventory Match relies on dispensary staff keeping exclusions up to date. Automatic, live inventory integration with a dispensary’s POS is in development and is not yet available. For more information, visit acannability.com.

What are Adverse Findings, and how are they different from therapeutic findings?+

Adverse Findings are documented safety signals, risk associations, known side effects, or trials that found no benefit, from peer-reviewed scientific literature. They are graded on the same A–D evidence scale used for therapeutic findings, so users can assess their scientific strength. Every health topic presents them the same way — one evidence-graded, cited format across the whole resource, so no condition looks more or less serious than the evidence warrants. Any molecule with a documented finding for the topic you selected is also highlighted in red on the grid.

Molecules with documented adverse findings display a red ⚠ badge on their tile. Clicking the tile shows an Adverse Findings section in the detail panel with a plain-language summary and direct PubMed citation links.

Important: The absence of a ⚠ badge does not mean a molecule is safe — most cannabis molecules have not yet been sufficiently studied for adverse effects. As new research emerges, additional molecules will be flagged. Some citations with weak study designs (e.g., ecological studies) appear as footnotes rather than full adverse entries, per Acannability editorial policy.

Why can the same product affect two people differently?+

Because people are not interchangeable. How much of a cannabis molecule reaches your bloodstream — and how long it stays there — varies from person to person, so the same product at the same dose can affect two people differently. Factors include genetics (inherited differences in the liver enzymes that process cannabinoids), metabolism, prior cannabis exposure (regular use can change sensitivity over time), route of administration (inhaled, oral, sublingual, topical and transdermal forms differ substantially in how much reaches the bloodstream and how fast), concurrent medications, and individual bioavailability.

You will find this stated in three places: on any molecule tile you open, on the Guided Match recommendation, and on every printout. Published findings describe what researchers observed in study populations and should not be interpreted as predicting how any individual will respond. This is educational information, not dosing guidance.

How does inventory matching work, and what is coming next?+

Today, matching is manual and honest about it: pick a health topic, and the Associated Molecules panel lists every molecule published research links to it. Use ⚙ Refine Inventory Match to remove molecules or whole categories your dispensary does not carry, and the match updates instantly. Dispensary staff can also import a stock list as a CSV.

What is coming is automation. With a point-of-sale connection, in-stock ranking becomes live instead of manual. With certificate-of-analysis (COA) data, matching reaches past cannabinoids into the terpene profile, which is where most of the differentiation actually sits. Both are previewed in Demo Mode today.

One honest limit worth knowing: dispensary menus publish cannabinoid content for every product, terpene content for some, and flavonoid content for none. Where a product publishes no lab data for a molecule, The Table reports that it cannot verify a match rather than guessing.

What is the Entourage Effect and how is it displayed in this table?+

The Entourage Effect is a widely discussed concept in cannabis pharmacology describing how the many molecules of the cannabis plant—cannabinoids, terpenes, and flavonoids—may work together synergistically to produce effects that are greater or different than any single isolated compound. The idea was popularized by Dr. Raphael Mechoulam and has influenced how consumers, clinicians, and product developers think about whole-plant versus isolate therapies. It remains a hypothesis: most of the supporting research is preclinical, and a combined clinical benefit has not been established.

In The Table, the Entourage Effect explorer, Potential Molecular Interactions (the ⬢ Entourage Effect button in the header toolbar), lets users choose a health topic and see a proposed combination of molecules, the receptor systems each may engage, and how strong the underlying evidence is. Most proposed combinations are supported by preclinical or limited human research. This feature is intended for educational exploration and is based on published scientific literature reviewed by Acannability.

How should this chart be used by consumers?+

The Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™ chart is used as a common language for cannabis consumers and industry participants to promote a more informed and science-based conversation about the benefits of the cannabis plant. Some of the most common uses are as follows:

Product Selection. The chart can benefit conversation between consumers and their healthcare provider on which molecules are known or believed to address their desired use. The individual molecules shown can be used to compare product claims as shown on product labels.

Molecule Identification. The chart allows for easy identification of molecules and their properties. Clicking any molecule tile quickly accesses the molecule’s name, atomic mass, evidence rating, receptors, therapeutic indications, and published research.

Chemical Nomenclature. When naming chemical compounds, the chart may be consulted to determine the symbols and molecular masses of cannabis-derived compounds.

Understanding Trends. As the cannabis industry continues to mature, the Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™ chart will be updated to reflect the molecules of current interest by consumers and the industry.

Research and Experimentation. Scientists and researchers may use the chart as a reference when investigating cannabis compounds or reviewing published literature via the linked article PDFs.

Education. In educational settings, the chart may be used to introduce students and practitioners to the fundamental compounds of the cannabis plant and their known pharmacological activities.

Is this chart proprietary to Acannability?+

Yes. The Cannabis Periodic Table of Molecules™ chart was developed by Acannability through the work of its Advisor Joseph Friedman, RPh, MBA. It is free to use by Acannability members and available at no charge to others by a simple copyright license acknowledgement. A printable version of the chart is available at Acannability.com.
